column1: # clues.tsv for rush01 — pedagogic hints only. NEVER state the expected value or the fix.
# Format: <hint><TAB><member CASE label>...; most-fundamental first. All MEMBER-LESS, so
# every hint fires on any failing case: rush01 is a program, each invocation is its own
# test, and a table's CASE column is a line number with nothing to key a hint on (c-11 ex05).
# Keep this block short: tools/rush01_check.sh prints the file verbatim, comments included.

Start with the GOT column, because the subject fixes the shape of a correct answer down to the byte: one line per row of the grid, the four digits of that row separated by single spaces, and a newline ending every row — including the last one. That is why the subject shows its example through `| cat -e`: every `$` in that transcript marks a newline it expects, and there is nothing else in the output at all. No banner, no blank line at the end, no space left dangling before a newline.

The program is handed exactly ONE argument, and that argument is one string holding sixteen values. Anything else is, in the subject's own words, an error: no argument at all, a second argument, fifteen values, seventeen, or a token that is not a single digit between '1' and '4'. And the subject fixes exactly one thing to print for every one of those situations — the word Error and a newline, nothing more, with no clue as to which check tripped and no difference between "you gave me nonsense" and "this puzzle has no solution". This harness reads it from the same stream it reads the grid from. So before trusting the string: how many arguments did your program actually receive, and how many values were really inside the one it read?

Two rules have to hold at the same time, and the sixteen numbers you were given are only the second of them. The first is the grid itself: every row and every column must contain each height exactly once, so no height may appear twice in any row or in any column. A grid that answers all sixteen views but repeats a height in a row is not a solution, and the sweep checks that rule on every grid your program prints.

A view is a COUNT of how many boxes you can see from one end of a row or a column — not a sum, not a position, not a height. Walking in from that end, a box is visible only if every box you have already walked past is shorter than it: the subject's own example is a row where the box of height 3 hides the box of height 1 behind it, so that side sees 3 boxes and not 4. Take one row of the grid your program printed, count its two views by hand, then do the same for one column, and compare those four numbers with the four you were handed.
